questions.question: What's the difference between strings and symbols in Ruby?
questions.title: Strings vs Symbols in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Strings are mutable text: 'hello', "world #{name}". Symbols are immutable, interned identifiers: :hello. The key differences: a new 'hello' each time creates a new String object; :hello is the same object every time (interned — one copy in memory). Strings are for data you'll display or change; symbols are for identifiers (hash keys, method names, config keys) — they're memory-efficient and compare by identity. Hash keys: {:name => 'Ada'} uses symbols (efficient); {'name' => 'Ada'} uses strings (a new string each time). Comparison: 'a' == 'a' compares value; :a == :a compares identity (same object). Symbols aren't strings — you can't concatenate (:a + :b raises), but :a.to_s gives 'a' and 'a'.to_sym gives :a. Use symbols for keys/identifiers, strings for text.

sections.title: String vs Symbol
sections.content:
String = mutable text (new object each time); Symbol = immutable interned identifier (same object). Strings for text; symbols for keys.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[String 'hello'] --> M[mutable; new object each time]
  Sy[Symbol :hello] --> I[immutable; same object]
  S --> U[use for text]
```

sections.title: Strings and symbols
sections.content:
```ruby
# String: mutable text (new object each time)
a = 'hello'
b = 'hello'
a.object_id == b.object_id   # false (different objects)
a + ' world'                  # 'hello world' (concatenation ok)
"#{1 + 1}"                     # '2' (interpolation in double quotes)

# Symbol: immutable, interned identifier (SAME object every time)
x = :hello
y = :hello
x.object_id == y.object_id   # true (same object — interned)
# :a + :b                      # raises (can't concatenate symbols)
:hello.to_s                   # 'hello' (symbol -> string)
'hello'.to_sym                # :hello (string -> symbol)

# Hash keys: symbols (efficient) vs strings (new string each time)
h = { name: 'Ada', age: 30 }   # { :name => 'Ada', :age => 30 }  (symbols)
h[:name]                       # 'Ada'
# A string key is a DIFFERENT key:
h2 = { 'name' => 'Ada' }
h2[:name]                      # nil  (string key != symbol key)

# Use SYMBOLS for keys/identifiers (efficient, compare by identity);
# use STRINGS for text you display or change.
```
